# Memory-recall golden set

The fixture behind `tests/test_memory_recall_eval_db.py`, from plan
`2026-07-29-memory-recall-efficacy-benchmark`. It answers the question no
existing memory metric answers: **did retrieval return the right thing, and
what did it cost?**

Reviewed like code. Grows when a real recall failure is found — every
"memory should have caught that" incident becomes a case.

## Files

| File | Holds |
|---|---|
| `manifest.json` | Format version + `embedding_source` (vector provenance) |
| `records.json` | The corpus to seed — one object per record |
| `cases.json` | The `(query, relevant, rationale)` triples to score |

### `records.json`

```json
{
  "key": "stable-local-identifier",
  "title": "…",
  "content": "…",
  "kind": "reference",
  "importance": 0.8,
  "embedding": [384 floats]        // optional — see provenance below
}
```

`key` is a fixture-local name, **not** a `memory_id`. Real ids are assigned
by Postgres at seed time, so the fixture cannot know them; the harness maps
returned ids back to keys after seeding.

### `cases.json`

```json
{
  "case_id": "corr-sccache-wrapper",
  "query_text": "how do I escape a stuck sccache build",
  "relevant": ["sccache-wedge-correction", "sccache-wedge-original"],
  "class": "correction",
  "correction": {"corrector": "…", "corrected": "…"},   // correction cases only
  "rationale": "why these records are the right answer",
  "query_embedding": [384 floats]                        // optional
}
```

`class` is one of `correction`, `vocabulary_mismatch`, `recency_conflict`,
`general` — the three hard classes the plan names, plus everything else.
Scores are reported per class as well as in aggregate, because a headline
recall number that hides a collapsed vocabulary-mismatch bucket is worse
than no number.

`correction.corrector` must also appear in `relevant`, or precedence and
recall would disagree about the same case. The loader rejects that.

## Vector provenance — read before interpreting a hybrid number

`manifest.json`'s `embedding_source` decides what the hybrid arm's numbers
*mean*:

| Tag | Vectors | Hybrid numbers mean |
|---|---|---|
| `hashing-stub-v1` | Not committed; derived at seed time | Fusion **mechanics** only |
| `minilm-l6-v2-256@sentence-transformers` | Committed in the fixture | Real **semantic retrieval quality** |

**This fixture now carries real vectors** (`minilm-l6-v2-256@sentence-transformers`),
generated by `regenerate_vectors.py` against the runner's local embedding
service — the same service that embeds the corpus, so query and record land in
the same space by construction.

How much the stub was understating: on the identical case set, the
`vocabulary_mismatch` class scored Recall@10 **0.300** under the stub and
**0.900** with real vectors. A stub number is not a conservative estimate of
the real one — it is a different measurement, and it happened to be wrong in
the direction that would have made semantic retrieval look barely worth doing.

The stub is a hashed bag-of-words: two texts sharing no content words land
near-orthogonal under it, exactly like full-text search. So every
`vocabulary_mismatch` case — the class that exists specifically to measure
what semantic retrieval buys — is **unmeasurable** under the stub tag. It
will score near zero on both arms and that is an artifact of the stub, not
a finding about the system.

The harness enforces this rather than trusting a reader to remember it: it
refuses to label a run's numbers as semantic-quality unless the manifest
claims the deployed space **and** vectors are actually committed.

### Regenerating with real vectors

The backend embeds nothing, by design — `app/services/memory_vectors.py`
holds constants and validation only, and `tests/test_no_fastembed_import.py`
bans the model from coming back. So real vectors are always produced
**out-of-band by a runner** (which pays for its own compute) and committed
here as data. That is what keeps the harness deterministic and identical
across machines: the vectors are in the tree, not recomputed per run.

To regenerate:

1. Embed every `records.json` `content` and every `cases.json` `query_text`
   with the deployed model, in the space named by `EMBEDDING_MODEL_TAG`.
2. Write each 384-float vector to the record's `embedding` and the case's
   `query_embedding`. All-or-nothing — the loader rejects a partially
   embedded corpus, because a hybrid arm scoring a subset while the
   full-text arm scores everything makes the two arms incomparable.
3. Flip `manifest.json`'s `embedding_source` to the model tag.
4. Re-run the harness and re-record the baseline in the plan's §3 Phase 2.

Changing the deployed model tag invalidates the committed vectors: the
spaces are not interchangeable. Treat a tag change as requiring a fixture
regeneration in the same change.

## Growing the set

The plan targets 50–150 cases. The set shipped here is the **initial seed**
(24 cases over 30 records) covering all four classes end to end. Two
sourcing veins, in order of preference:

1. **Corrections already in the corpus.** Records whose titles begin
   `CORRECTION` / `CORRECTED` / `SUPERSEDED` are free labelled pairs —
   querying the old topic *must* surface the corrector, and rank it above
   what it corrects. Where `superseded_by` is populated it is the better
   join than title matching.
2. **Real recall failures.** When a session says "memory should have caught
   that", the query it actually issued becomes a case and the record it
   should have returned becomes the judgement.

Keep the corpus and the cases in one change: a case naming a record key
that does not exist is rejected at load, loudly, rather than scoring a
silent zero that reads exactly like a retrieval regression.
